html:
The fairs of Piacenza were meetings, held four times a year in the northern Italian town of Piacenza from 1579, where Genoese bankers and their partners settled bills of exchange from across Europe. There were almost no goods and few coins: it was a fair reduced to pure credit.

A bill of exchange was a written order to pay a sum at another place, usually in another currency, at a later date. Merchants used them to move money without shipping coin, and bankers used them to lend. The fairs had started at Besançon, which is why they were still called the Bisenzone fairs after they moved, and they settled at Piacenza in 1579.

How a fair ran:

  • A few dozen bankers, mostly Genoese, took part, with others from Florence and Milan.
  • They brought in the bills falling due and offset them against each other, so that only small balances were paid in cash.
  • They agreed the exchange rates for the next fair, and set new bills running.

Through these fairs the silver of the Spanish empire, landing at Seville, was turned into payments for Spanish troops in Flanders. They were the clearing house of Genoa's age at the centre, and Fernand Braudel counts them among the most advanced money markets of their time. They declined in the 1620s, when Spain's finances and the Genoese hold on them weakened, and the lead passed to the Amsterdam Exchange.
